# Do you need a check-up every six months? {#sec-recall}

Almost everyone in Britain believes they should see a dentist every six months.
It is one of the most successful pieces of health messaging ever devised, and
nobody can quite say where it came from. The best available accounts trace it to
mid-twentieth-century convention and to marketing, not to research.

It has now been tested. This chapter is about what happened, and about the odd
fact that the guideline has not caught up with it.

## The advice

> Assign a recall interval ranging from 3 to 24 months, based on oral health needs
> and disease risk
>
> Strength of recommendation: **Conditional**
>
> --- *Delivering Better Oral Health*, chapter 2, table 1f [@dboh2025]

For children the range is 3 to 12 months.

Notice what this actually says: it does **not** say six months. It says
risk-based, anywhere from three months to two years. The guideline has already
moved away from the six-month rule; it is the profession and the public who have
not.

## What the guideline says its evidence is

> Recommendation based on **very low certainty evidence**. Recommendation in line
> with NICE (CG19).
>
> --- *Delivering Better Oral Health*, chapter 13 [@dboh2025]

NICE CG19 is *Dental checks: intervals between oral health reviews* [@niceCG19].
It was published in **2004**.

## Following the citation, and finding it is out of date

The Cochrane review DBOH cites alongside NICE is Fee and colleagues, updated in
2020 [@fee2020]. It includes two studies with data from 1,736 participants. The
larger is the INTERVAL trial, conducted in UK general dental practices in adults
who were regular attenders, comparing 6-month, 24-month and risk-based recall,
with outcomes at **four years**.

Here is what it found.

| Comparison | Outcome | Effect | 95% CI | Certainty |
|:-------------------|:------------------------|:-----------|:--------------|:-------------|
| **Risk-based vs 6-month** | tooth surfaces with any caries | MD 0.15 | −0.77 to 1.08 | [high]{.certainty .high} |
| Risk-based vs 6-month | % sites with gingival bleeding | MD 0.78% | −1.17% to 2.73% | [high]{.certainty .high} |
| Risk-based vs 6-month | quality of life (OHIP-14) | MD −0.35 | −1.02 to 0.32 | [high]{.certainty .high} |
| Risk-based vs 6-month | moderate-to-extensive caries | RR 1.04 | 0.99 to 1.09 | [moderate]{.certainty .moderate} |
| **24-month vs 6-month** | tooth surfaces with any caries | MD −0.60 | −2.54 to 1.34 | [moderate]{.certainty .moderate} |
| 24-month vs 6-month | quality of life (OHIP-14) | MD −0.24 | −1.55 to 1.07 | [high]{.certainty .high} |

: Recall intervals in adults, four-year follow-up [@fee2020] {#tbl-recall}

Read the certainty column. **High.** Repeatedly.

This is, along with [Chapter -@sec-scale-polish], one of only two places in this
entire book where I have found high-certainty evidence, and both of them are
findings of **no important difference**. Adults who attended every six months did
not end up with fewer decayed surfaces, less gum bleeding, or better
oral-health-related quality of life than adults on risk-based or two-yearly
recall. The intervals are narrow and centred near zero, which as
[Chapter -@sec-scale-polish] explains is a real answer rather than an empty
literature.

## The part that is genuinely odd

DBOH rates this recommendation **very low certainty**.

The Cochrane review it cites contains **high**-certainty evidence for three
patient-relevant outcomes.

I do not think this is carelessness, and there is a reading that makes sense of
it. Fee 2020 provides high-certainty evidence that **lengthening intervals does
not harm** low-risk regular attenders. It provides very little about what the
*optimal* interval is for any given person, or about children, where the only
evidence is one small Norwegian study with very low certainty. If DBOH's "very
low" refers to the evidence supporting a **risk-based assignment across the 3-to-24
month range**, rather than to the specific comparisons the trial ran, then it is
defensible.

But that is my reconstruction, not the guideline's statement. And the practical
effect of writing "very low certainty" against this row is to understate what is
now known. A dentist reading chapter 13 would reasonably conclude that the
evidence on recall intervals is thin. It is thin for the specific question of
personalising the interval. It is not thin at all for the question the public
actually cares about, which is whether six-monthly is necessary.

Add to that the deferral to a guideline from **2004**, which predates the INTERVAL
trial entirely, and this row reads as one the 2025 update did not revisit.

::: {.callout-note title="How I judged this: the population matters" collapse="true"}
Who was in these trials? Adults who were **regular attenders**, defined as having
seen a dentist at least once in the previous two years, in UK general practice.
Children in the other study were also regular attenders, in a Norwegian public
dental service.

So the finding is: among people who already go to the dentist and have reasonably
looked-after mouths, going twice a year rather than less often does not improve
outcomes over four years.

It says nothing about people who do not attend, who have untreated disease, or
who are at high risk. For them the whole question is different, and the answer is
probably that they need to be seen more, not less.

**What was not measured.** Neither study measured other potential adverse effects.
And four years is not long for a disease that develops over decades. The review is
explicit about both.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="What I searched, and when" collapse="true"}
PubMed, 21 August 2026, for updates to CD004346. The 2020 version (`.pub5`)
remains current.

I have the full text of the Cochrane review, its characteristics of included
studies, the INTERVAL main trial report and the NIHR HTA monograph, all supplied
during writing. The HTA monograph contains the cost analysis, which I have not
audited.

Full record in `appraisals/searches/ch28-recall.md`.
:::

::: {.verdict}
[Verdict]{.verdict-title}

Certainty of evidence
:   [High]{.certainty .high} that, for adults who attend regularly, risk-based or
    24-month recall produces no important difference from 6-month recall in
    caries, gingival bleeding or oral-health-related quality of life over four
    years. [Very low]{.certainty .very-low} for children, from one small study.

    **This is higher than DBOH's stated rating**, and the discrepancy is the
    finding of this chapter.

Directness to the advice as worded
:   **Excellent for the six-month question, poor for the risk-based question.**
    The trial compared exactly the intervals people argue about, with
    patient-relevant outcomes, over four years, in general practice. What it
    cannot tell you is how to assign an individual to a point on a 3-to-24 month
    range, which is what the recommendation actually asks clinicians to do.

Is the strength label defensible?
:   **Conditional is right; the certainty rating is not.** Rating this very low,
    and deferring to a 2004 NICE guideline, understates high-certainty evidence
    that the six-month default is unnecessary for regular attenders. This is the
    only place in the book where I think the guideline is **too pessimistic** about
    its own evidence, and the effect is to leave an outdated norm unchallenged.

What would change my mind
:   Evidence that four years is too short and differences emerge later. Evidence
    in irregular attenders or high-risk groups, where I would expect the answer to
    reverse. And any trial actually testing risk-based assignment tools against
    each other, which would address the question DBOH's rating seems to be about.
:::

## What this means for you

If you are an adult who goes to the dentist reasonably regularly and your mouth
is in decent shape, there is high-certainty evidence that you do not need to go
every six months. Going less often, or on a schedule your dentist sets based on
your actual risk, produced no measurable difference over four years in decay,
bleeding gums, or how your mouth felt.

The national guideline already says this: 3 to 24 months, based on need. Six
months is not in it.

Two caveats. If you have untreated decay or gum disease, or you rarely attend,
none of this applies to you; the trials were in people who were already doing
fine. And in England, whether you can *get* an appointment is a more pressing
constraint than how often you should want one.
